extracted.intended_audience: policy scholars, regulatory researchers, and regulatory practitioners interested in notice-and-comment influence on science use
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing which features of public comments influence the scientific citations included or removed in EPA Regulatory Impact Analyses (RIAs). The paper analyzes commenter types, textual alignment, and coordination patterns that affect citation changes between RIA versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commenter Type Matters Most
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenter Type Matters Most — Members of Congress and industry groups demonstrated the strongest effect on which scientific citations appeared in revised RIAs; individual citizens and interest groups showed minimal measurable influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Who submits the comment is the single strongest predictor of influence on RIA citations. Comments from Members of Congress and organized industry groups are far more likely to affect which studies are cited in revised regulatory analyses. Individual citizens and interest groups have much weaker measurable impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire Alarm Pattern / Congressional Echo
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Fire Alarm' pattern: When industry commenters raised concerns about specific studies, Members of Congress would echo those concerns, prompting EPA officials to remove challenged citations from revised documents—even when the final rule itself remained unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordination or echoing between industry and congressional actors amplifies influence: targeted industry challenges that are mirrored by Members of Congress increase the chance that EPA will drop contested citations. For practitioners, eliciting congressional attention can be an instrumentally effective pathway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted Challenges to Specific Studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that raised concerns about specific studies were especially likely to lead to removal of those challenged citations from revised RIAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific, study-level critiques (naming particular papers/methods/results) are more consequential than general objections. If the goal is to affect which scientific evidence is cited, focus comments on concrete, targeted methodological or factual problems in named studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation inclusion/exclusion in RIAs (outcome metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study tracks which scientific citations are added to or dropped from successive versions of an RIA as the primary observable outcome of comment influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measuring comment effectiveness can be operationalized by comparing citation lists across RIA versions: additions, deletions, and persistence of citations indicate how agency science use changed following the comment period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual similarity between comments and RIA abstracts/citations
rubrics_metrics.description: The researchers measured similarity between comment text and RIA content; e.g., 'Abstracts added to later RIA versions showed approximately 55% lower similarity with comments from Congress members and industry compared to citations that were dropped.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual alignment (similarity) between comment language and RIA wording is used as an empirical indicator of influence. This metric can reveal whether RIA text reflects comment framing or wording; the paper reports notable differences in similarity tied to added vs. dropped citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of citing research within comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups were most likely to cite research (42% included citations), yet had negligible measurable influence on which citations appeared in RIAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including citations in comments is common among interest groups and may signal evidence-based engagement, but frequency of citing research alone does not guarantee influence. The actor citing the research and other dynamics (e.g., political leverage) matter more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence Quality Paradox (who cites vs. influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence Quality Paradox: Interest groups cited research most frequently but had negligible influence; industry groups cited less frequently but wielded disproportionate power when they did comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The credibility or quantity of evidence supplied by itself may not determine influence—political positioning and actor type can outweigh apparent evidence quality. Evaluators should account for actor influence asymmetries when interpreting citation changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual factors: rule salience and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Study Limitation: analysis examined a single salient rule during a science-friendly administration, limiting generalizability to broader rulemaking patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The political and administrative context (e.g., salience of the rule, orientation of the administration) conditions how comments affect agency science use. Findings from a single, high-salience case under a science-friendly administration may not generalize across rules or administrations.
